clue.text: Professional adds up money

definitions.note: 'Money' is a mass noun standing in for a plural: any amount of it counts, while the answer is the countable word for what a business clears.

parts.note: PRO is the short form a professional golfer or footballer goes by
when a story adds up it fits — the two phrases mean the same

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an accountant at work, which is exactly where 'adds up' belongs; read as wordplay it is a plain synonym instead.
explanation.definitionFit: money -> PROFITS: what a business clears once costs are paid, so the general word points at one particular sort of takings.

clue.text: Good, cheap cigarette papers, ultimately they're for smoking tobacco

definitions.note: The setter defines by function and by a whole clause: 'they're for smoking tobacco' says what the plural answer is used for rather than naming a noun you could swap in.

parts.note: PI is short for pious, the crossword's good in the sanctimonious sense

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so each word in the list before it hands over its final letter and nothing else.

parts.note: the closing letters of the three words, in the order they are given

explanation.walkthrough: PI for 'good' is worth banking — it is pious cut down, and a setter drops it in without warning. The comma list after it is quiet letter-work.
explanation.definitionFit: they’re for smoking tobacco -> PIPES: the bowl-and-stem kind a smoker fills and lights, named by the job they do rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Determined to put on exhaust

parts.note: someone out to win is set on winning, so out carries the determination
clothes you put on are clothes you wear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Determined to put on' reads as one phrase about getting dressed, and splits into two unrelated senses the moment you stop reading it as English.
explanation.definitionFit: exhaust -> OUTWEAR: to outwear something is to wear it out, using it until nothing is left — which is what exhausting a supply or a person means.

clue.text: Club batting, accepting run out

indicators.note: Whatever accepts something takes it inside itself, so these letters open up and let the next pair sit in the middle.

parts.note: a batsman at the crease is said to be in
RO is the scorer's shorthand beside a dismissal of that kind

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket runs through the whole surface, and the definition has quietly walked off to a different sport where the clubs are numbered.
explanation.definitionFit: Club -> IRON: the metal-headed golf clubs are the irons, so the general word is pointing at one particular kind of club.

clue.text: True American siren chasing pure son

definitions.note: 'American' is not part of the person described — it flags where the idiom is spoken — and 'true' is an adjective doing duty for a noun phrase.

indicators.note: One thing chasing another runs along behind it, so the piece doing the chasing takes up the rear of the assembly.

parts.note: spirits drunk with nothing added are drunk straight, so straight is undiluted
S is son on a family tree
a hooter is the siren that sounds over a factory

explanation.walkthrough: The siren is a hooter, the noisy sort on a factory roof, and the fifteen letters run across the whole grid because two of the three pieces are ordinary words.
explanation.definitionFit: True American -> STRAIGHT SHOOTER: US idiom for one who deals honestly and says what they mean, shooting straight rather than crooked.

clue.text: Model paper plane's not one

indicators.note: Not is the plainest removal instruction there is: whatever follows it is missing from the word standing before it.

parts.note: the paper you sit in a hall is an exam
'one' here is the indefinite article, and these are the letters that go missing
PLANE with that article struck out of its middle

explanation.walkthrough: 'One' as the indefinite article is the piece of vocabulary to bank: a setter can write one and mean nothing more than A or AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Model -> EXAMPLE: the specimen held up to be copied — 'a model of restraint' is someone being offered as one.

clue.text: Forces show terrible drug being cut: heroin put into skin with needle

indicators.note: A word that has been cut has had a piece taken off the end, so its last letter never reaches the assembly.
Something terrible is in a bad state, and letters in a bad state are not left in the order the clue handed them over.

parts.note: four letters of fodder, taken as they stand
BEING docked of its last letter gives four more
H is heroin in the crossword's drug shorthand
ink put into skin with a needle names the second word outright, no letters required

explanation.walkthrough: Half the answer is spelled out of letters and half is simply defined, which is why the clue changes gear at the colon. A military tattoo is a display, not a drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Forces show -> EDINBURGH TATTOO: the massed military display staged on the castle esplanade each August, mounted by the armed services.

clue.text: Writing this, hour wasted filling a puzzle at the beginning

indicators.note: Time wasted is time laid to ruin, and ruined letters do not keep the order they arrived in.
What fills a space sits inside it, so this material beds down between the two pieces on either side.
Only what stands at the front is wanted, so the word beside it gives up its opening letter alone.

parts.note: the clue's own a, taken as a single letter
eight letters of fodder waiting to be reordered
the opening letter of puzzle and no more of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Writing this' looks like the setter at his desk complaining about the hour, and 'this' turns out to be raw material rather than a reference to the crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing -> AUTHORSHIP: the fact of having written something, as in 'the authorship of the letter is disputed' — who did the writing.

clue.text: One trying to flog something is a tosser

definitions.meaning: to flog is to sell, and a salesman's spiel is his sales pitch
in baseball, the player who throws the ball at the batter

explanation.walkthrough: The British insult buried in 'tosser' is the trap: the clue means the word literally, and both halves land on someone who throws.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are people who throw — the salesman throws his pitch at a customer, the baseball player throws the ball at the batter.

clue.text: Back horse with tip for the first from Haydock

indicators.note: Putting one thing in for another is a swap, so what precedes it moves into the place the letter named after it was holding.

parts.note: the tip of a thing is its far END
HORSE with the letter it starts on given away
the letter that steps aside is the one Haydock opens on

explanation.walkthrough: Haydock is a racecourse, so the horse and the tip belong to the same afternoon — and 'tip' turns out to mean an extremity, not a hot prospect.
explanation.definitionFit: Back -> ENDORSE: to endorse a candidate is to put your name behind them publicly, which is what backing someone amounts to.

clue.text: Pocket tip and mostly split collection

indicators.note: Most of a word is all of it bar the final letter, so the word beside this one arrives one letter short.

parts.note: to pot a ball at snooker is to pocket it
to tip a jug is to pour from it
to split cloth is to RIP it, and the last letter is left behind

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' is a verb here, as it is nowhere else in this puzzle, and the French original of the answer means, aptly enough, rotten pot.
explanation.definitionFit: collection -> POTPOURRI: a jar of mixed dried petals, and by extension any miscellany — an assortment of unlike things rather than a matched set.

clue.text: Did carry tons having ends of feet on either side

indicators.note: What has something on either side of it has been split to make room, half the letters landing to the left and half to the right.

parts.note: the ends of feet are toes, so whatever has them is described as toed
T is the standard abbreviation for tons

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has someone hauling a load with toes poking out on both sides; the wordplay is the same picture with one letter wedged in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Did carry -> TOTED: to tote is to lug something about, as in 'tote that barge', so the past tense answers 'did carry'.

clue.text: Descendants to get diamonds

definitions.note: 'Descendants' is plural and the answer is a collective singular — one word covering an entire line of them, as in 'the seed of Abraham'.

parts.note: to get a joke is to see it
D is diamonds at the bridge table

explanation.walkthrough: Cards supply the last letter, as they so often do, and 'get' has to be read as understanding rather than obtaining.
explanation.definitionFit: Descendants -> SEED: the biblical sense of the word, where a man's seed is his offspring and every generation after him.

clue.text: Ubiquitous leader is great alongside fellow union member

indicators.note: Set alongside means set next to, so the two pieces stand shoulder to shoulder in the order the clue names them.

parts.note: a great tree and a big tree are the same tree
trade unionists have addressed one another that way since the movement began

explanation.walkthrough: The union convention is the one to bank here, and it keeps the whole surface at a shop-floor meeting where nobody is watching anybody.
explanation.definitionFit: Ubiquitous leader -> BIG BROTHER: Orwell's 1984 gave the ever-watching head of state a name now used for any authority you cannot get away from.

clue.text: Thought before entering bet, card getting dealt

indicators.note: To enter a room is to go inside it, so this short word lands within the letters that surround it.
Cards being dealt come off the pack in no particular order, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, taken from the two words together
ERE is the poet's word for before, and it drops in once the rest is shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: The card table in the surface is a decoy for a word about brains, and 'before' is the shortest bit of poetic vocabulary a setter can slip past you.
explanation.definitionFit: Thought -> CEREBRATED: to cerebrate is to use the cerebrum, that is to think, and the past tense matches 'thought' as the past of think.

clue.text: Awkward delivery bowled here; front of crease is rough

indicators.note: The front of a word is the letter it starts on, so only that one is taken from what follows.
Rough ground is uneven and unsorted, and letters left rough have not been smoothed into the order they came in.

parts.note: b is how a scorecard records a batsman bowled
four letters of fodder, taken as they stand
the leading letter of crease joins the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: Two kinds of delivery in one word: the ball bowled at the crease, and the birth the definition means. Only one of them is awkward.
explanation.definitionFit: Awkward delivery -> BREECH: a birth in which the baby arrives bottom-first, the hard way round, is a breech presentation.

clue.text: Soldiers wait on order

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the crossword's standing regiment
to wait on a table is to serve it

explanation.walkthrough: Three military-sounding words in a row and only the first is doing army work; the surface reads as soldiers awaiting instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: order -> RESERVE: to reserve a table is to order it kept for you, the booking sense of the verb rather than the commanding one.

clue.text: Conservative leader of yesteryear to hug tree

indicators.note: A word's leader is the letter at its head, so the noun after this hands over its first letter and stays out of the rest.

parts.note: C is the Conservative party on a ballot paper
the head of yesteryear, one letter only
to press someone to you is to hug them

explanation.walkthrough: A Tory grandee from the old days is the picture, and two single letters is all the clue wants of him before the embrace.
explanation.definitionFit: tree -> CYPRESS: the dark evergreen conifer of Mediterranean churchyards, so the general word is pointing at one particular species.

clue.text: Vehicles over street with old wheels

indicators.note: One thing laid over another covers it, so these letters close around what follows instead of stacking on top of it.

parts.note: the commonest vehicles of all, and they part in the middle
ST is street on any envelope
O is old, as in Old English

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' tempts you to stack the pieces one above the next; here it means covering, the way a coat goes over a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: wheels -> CASTORS: the little swivelling wheels screwed under furniture so a chair or a trolley rolls wherever it is pushed.

clue.text: Common cold going round pub, endlessly

indicators.note: Something going round another thing encircles it, so these letters part and close again on what comes next.
Without its end, the word beside this hands over everything except its final letter.

parts.note: the polar regions are the cold ends of the earth
PUB stripped of its last letter is what goes inside

explanation.walkthrough: The common cold is one illness in the surface and two separate jobs in the wordplay, which is what makes the phrase so easy to read straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: Common -> POPULAR: both mean of the people at large — popular opinion is common opinion, the Latin populus sense rather than 'well liked'.

clue.text: Perhaps one in stock here if wanting order

indicators.note: To want something is to lack it, so letters wanting order can be put back in any other arrangement.

parts.note: six letters of fodder, taken from the two words as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the setter admitting the definition is only an example, and the shopkeeper's sense of 'in stock' is there to keep you off the farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Perhaps one in stock -> HEIFER: livestock is stock on a farm, and a young cow that has not calved is one instance of it.

clue.text: Summary in short, great book

indicators.note: Something given in short is cut down, so the word governed by this loses its last letter before joining on.

parts.note: an epic is great in scale, and it arrives a letter short
a tome is a weighty book

explanation.walkthrough: Everyday English uses this word for a perfect specimen; the clue wants the original bookish sense, which is also why a tome turns up in the build.
explanation.definitionFit: Summary -> EPITOME: the older sense of the word, an abstract or condensed version of a longer work, rather than 'the perfect specimen of'.

clue.text: She flies American back every week to country

indicators.note: Back sends an across answer's letters the other way along the row, right to left, so the piece it follows arrives turned round.

parts.note: the American is US, and it arrives facing the other way
per day means every day
W is the calendar's short form of week
the sultanate at the eastern end of the Arabian peninsula

explanation.walkthrough: The capital S of 'She' is fair warning that a named person is wanted, and everything after it is build — four pieces, only one of them a whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: She flies -> SUPERWOMAN: the comic-book heroine of the Superman family, whose powers include flight, with 'she' marking out the female one.

clue.text: Bills squeezing current benefits

indicators.note: Squeezing something in forces it between what is already there, so the single letter ends up inside the longer piece.

parts.note: a bill pasted up on a hoarding is an advert
I is the physicist's symbol for electric current

explanation.walkthrough: Bills are posters here rather than invoices, and the current is the one running down a wire — two everyday words both used in their second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: benefits -> AIDS: things that help, the way a hearing aid or a visual aid benefits whoever uses it, so both plurals name supports.

clue.text: '90s band did rock on the radio

indicators.note: What reaches you over the radio is heard and never seen, so the spelling is the solver's to work out from the sound alone.

parts.note: to rock back and forth is to sway, so 'did rock' is SWAYED — and that is the noise the answer makes

explanation.walkthrough: The material the band named itself after is spelt nothing like the word you say out loud, which is the whole point of hearing it broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: ‘90s band -> SUEDE: the Britpop group who opened the decade, so the definition names one particular band of those years.

clue.text: Spot fine, put up charges

indicators.note: Put up means raised, and in a down answer a raised assembly is read from the bottom of the column upwards.

parts.note: to spot something is to see it
F is fine on the side of a pencil

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a police caution — spot fine, charges brought — and every word of it means something else.
explanation.definitionFit: charges -> FEES: what a professional charges for services rendered, the money sense of 'charge' rather than the accusation or the cavalry's.

clue.text: Downed one water, drinking litre after round

indicators.note: Whatever is drinking takes something in, so the longer piece swallows the single letter named beside it.

parts.note: the round shape is the letter O

indicators.note: After the round means behind it, so that letter leads and the rest of the build follows on.

parts.note: the wet is water — the stuff you come in out of
L is the litre on a bottle label

explanation.walkthrough: Downed, drinking, water, litre, round: the surface is a heavy night at the pub, and the definition is about feathers rather than drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Downed one -> OWLET: a nestling owl still covered in down, so 'downed' describes its plumage and not anything drunk or knocked over.

clue.text: Lead championship with Ronaldo's header: that's great for Real Madrid fans?

parts.note: the championship a fighter or a club holds is the title

indicators.note: A header in football is played off the top of the head, so the top letter of the name beside it is what comes off.

parts.note: the head of the footballer's name

parts.words: that's great for Real Madrid fans?
parts.note: olé is the Spanish shout of approval a Madrid crowd would be roaring

explanation.walkthrough: Ronaldo and Real Madrid keep the surface on the pitch, and the last three letters are a crowd's shout rather than any English word.
explanation.definitionFit: Lead -> TITLE ROLE: the part a play is named after is its leading part, so whoever acts it has the lead.

clue.text: One steps over poo; shoe initially turned over

indicators.note: Taken initially, a word gives up only the letter it begins on and none of the rest.
Anything turned over ends up facing the way it came from, so the assembled letters are read from the far end back.

parts.note: a row over money is a row re money — over can mean concerning
dirt is what a dog leaves on the pavement
the first letter of shoe

explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' is the piece to bank: it can mean concerning, the RE of a memo heading, and spotting that is what breaks the pavement scene into letters.
explanation.definitionFit: One steps -> STRIDER: someone who walks in long steps, the -er ending turning the action into the person performing it.

clue.text: Tramp without clothes, sight is disgusting

indicators.note: Strip the clothes off a word and its outermost letters go with them, leaving only what they were covering.

parts.note: a tramp is a HOBO, and the two letters at his edges come off
a sight to behold is a scene

explanation.walkthrough: Tramp is this setter's own pseudonym, so he opens his last clue by undressing himself — and the whole surface stays in character.
explanation.definitionFit: disgusting -> OBSCENE: what offends decency outright; the word has widened from indecent to grossly excessive, as in obscene wealth.
